newsitem.title: albania: Albania government says south still out of control.
newsitem.headline: Albania government says south still out of control.

text.p: Albania's government moved to regain control of towns in the south of the Balkan state on Tuesday after a weekend of armed unrest, as President Sali Berisha met the political opposition over the crisis.
Security forces with orders to shoot armed protesters on sight have been moving south from Tirana to quash violence since a state of emergency was declared by parliament on Sunday.
The disorder erupted after a wave of protests, mainly in the south of Europe's poorest country, was sparked by the collapse in January of high-risk pyramid investment schemes.

The authorities said that the Adriatic port of Vlore and the coastal town of Sarande remained out of their control, despite a government ultimatum that forces would shoot without warning if weapons were not surrendered.
At least 19 people have been reported killed in the flashpoint town of Vlore since Friday.

Government officials said Albanian soldiers and police forces commanded the main north-south road as far as the hilltop town of Koshovice, beyond the weekend trouble spot of Fier and within 30 km (20 miles) of Vlore.
The Interior Ministry said residents in Fier had surrendered 1,500 weapons and a quantity of ammunition in accordance with a government ultimatum.
Further south the chaos showed little sign of ebbing and television reported "terrorists" in Vlore had killed four people on Monday as they tried to give up their guns.
In Vlore, scene of mass demonstrations over the past two months, a four-year-old girl was also killed by gunfire as she played in the garden of her home, television said.
The report, which could not be independently confirmed, said three other children in the port were wounded by explosives.

While security forces attempted to regain control, Albania's main opposition Socialist Party said it had appealed to Berisha at a meeting to agree to a new broad-based government to help end the violent unrest gripping the country.
But one of the Socialist leaders, Pandeli Majko, said the party had gained "no sense of compromise" at the talks.
"His (Berisha's) response was 'you must not try to take power by arms'," Majko told Reuters. "We advised him that we would never want power through blood," he said.
Officials in Berisha's ruling Democratic Party, whose leader Tritan Shehu was also at the talks according to Majko, were not immediately available for comment on the meeting.

The Democrat-controlled parliament declared the state of emergency after an announcement by Berisha, that his unpopular Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi would resign, failed to calm the southern disturbances.

Majko said he did not believe state of emergency measures could calm the situation. "It is no longer a matter of left or right but of protecting people and stopping further blood from being shed," he said of the call for a broad government.
Other state of emergency measures included a dusk-to-dawn curfew and tight controls on the media.
Western television broadcasts resumed from Albania after Tirana gave into criticism over kerbs on press freedom, a senior European Broadcasting Union (EBU) official in Geneva said.

It was the first suspension of EBU's links since 1989 when China interrupted Western images of the military crackdown at Tiananmen Square, according to Tony Naets, head of EBU's Eurovision News Services.

A Justice Ministry spokesman said journalists of foreign media organisations were free to report but advised against any travel to the south, where more than 20 people have been reported killed since Friday, mostly in Vlore.
Albanian television broadcast pictures of protesters in Sarande wearing goulish rubber masks on the deck of a navy minesweeper, firing weapons into the air.

Mourners in a village in the northern Tropoje district north of the capital buried a secret police officer killed in Vlore. State television showed a crowd of around 200 gathered at the graveside in the family's village of Cernik.
"My son Lek was killed but I call on all (Albanians) to lower the temperature, regardless of political affiliation. They should love Albania," the victim's father told television.
